fighter.name: Cass
fighter.background: Cass Mireles, 34. Grew up in a mining town in the Southwest and enlisted at 19; two deployments as an Army Ranger, then a discharge after a knee injury on a night jump. Worked as a hunting guide, then led a volunteer county search-and-rescue team. When the outbreak reached her county she was running the call at a roadblock, where the team was overrun.

entries.intro: Eli said an hour and it was three. I checked the fire and both ways out twice, put the knife into something dragging its feet at the edge of camp, and then he walked in with two rounds left and news of a house. I told him he was late. I also said thanks.
entries.mission1: Quiet first; rounds are for emergencies. If a cluster blocks the way, Eli runs, they follow, and I finish them from behind. He calls it being bait. He's not wrong, and he's the fastest thing I have.
entries.rescue: Six came out of the trees when we thought the house was clear, and I had nothing to put my back against but a wall. Two strangers with bows dropped every one. I gave them one night, because four hold a house better than two.
entries.base1: I told Eli about the pistol in my pack: empty, and out there a shot meant company. Tonight we can afford the noise. Door first, then everything else.
entries.herd: The birds went quiet. When the birds go quiet, something big is moving, and this wasn't one or two. I gave us two minutes and told everyone to seal what they could.
entries.done: Last one down. Eli, Ray, June, me: four counted, four standing. Eat, sleep. Tomorrow I find out how far we are from anything alive.

scout.name: Eli
scout.background: Eli Varga, 24. Grew up in a mountain town where the trails were the way out; ran his first ultramarathon at 17 and has finished several 100-mile races. Worked as a seasonal trail guide and a fire-lookout assistant, and has never been in a fight. He came down from his lookout station when the radio went silent, and met Cass at the roadblock.

entries.intro: I went up the ridge, found a house to the north, and came back with two rounds left and something right behind me. Cass said I was late, then thanked me, which I'm keeping. Then three more came out of the trees, and we stood still and let them walk into us.
entries.mission1: The plan: Cass stays quiet, I'm the bait, she finishes them. I run, they follow, and I'm winded after once per place. She called me fast, which is the nicest thing she's said to me.
entries.rescue: I said it was clear, and then there were six. I'll say it: I was scared. Then arrows, from two strangers, Ray and his daughter June, thirty days in the woods, and Cass gave them one night.
entries.base1: Rain on the way, so we fixed the door and the windows. Cass has had a pistol in her pack this whole time, of course she has. I'm not sure I know what I'm doing, but the door stayed shut.
entries.herd: The woods went silent and I couldn't hear anything, which Cass says is the point. Two minutes. I counted them, because counting helps. It didn't.
entries.done: We held. Against that. My legs are shaking and I could sleep standing, and for the first time in thirty days I think four is better than two.

hunter.name: Ray
hunter.background: Ray Bluestone, 40. Dakota, from a Dakota community in Minnesota, where he works as a tribal natural resources technician, counting deer and monitoring wild-rice lakes. Learned to hunt, track and read the woods from his grandfather and uncles, and runs the youth deer camp and archery lessons every fall. June is his daughter; they were bowhunting from a tree stand when the outbreak began, and have kept to the woods since.

entries.rescue: I watched the house from the trees since morning to see what kind of people they were. They worked quietly and didn't waste rounds, and when six came for them I stopped watching. June shot from too close again. I'll tell her again.
entries.base1: Rain building in the west, and nobody should be outside tonight. I counted arrows, eight each, and set traps, because four can hold a house if they plan before they go in. Cass wants one night. I'll try to make it more.
entries.herd: The birds stopped, and then the whole woods did. I know that silence from the stand, when something large is moving upwind. I told June to slow down and keep her arrows.
entries.done: The house held, and all four of us are still here. First night indoors in thirty days. June says I'm getting slow; I say I counted every arrow back.

archer.name: June
archer.background: June Bluestone, 15. Ray's daughter, in her second season hunting at his side; learned tracking and stillness from her grandfather and her dad, and is an excellent shot. She beads, sews her own ribbon-work trim, made her quilled knife sheath, carved her war club at a culture camp and knaps stone points. She was hunting with Ray when the outbreak began and has spent the thirty days since in the woods.

entries.rescue: I wanted to come down hours ago, but Dad wanted to know who they were. Six came out of the trees: four for me, two for him. I keep score.
entries.base1: Cass says fix the door first. Fine. Then I'm taking the room with the bed, because I called it.
entries.herd: Dad went still and said something big was coming. Good. I've waited thirty days for a real fight, and I've got eight arrows and a war club.
entries.done: We held. I'm keeping count and I'm ahead, whatever Dad says. Now I'm taking that bed.

tinkerer.name: Theo
tinkerer.role: IT and software worker, maths tutor
tinkerer.background: Theo Nakamura, 31. A remote IT and software worker who spent years fitting out his own house as a prepper's stash, with a bunker underneath, and tutored maths over video; June was one of his students. He was at home when the outbreak began. Squatters later took the house, and he sat sealed in the bunker with the power off until the squad got to him.

entries.bunker: I'd modelled that door opening a lot of ways, and my maths student walking in with her dad wasn't one of them. She's taller than on video. I'm out of food, so yes, I'm coming, sorry, one second, backpack.
entries.base2: Worst case, the squatters' friends come back; statistically, they come back. Plan A is barricades, Plan B is tripwires, and no, it isn't time to open the good case.
entries.hut: I traded cameras and wired alarms for a shack Ray built by hand. Nobody knows it exists, which might be the best security system I've seen. The good case came with me, still shut, because this isn't the real emergency yet.
